 AN CHÚIRT UACHTARACH 

 THE SUPREME COURT 

 S:AP:IE:2024:000124 

  [2026] IESC 2 

   

 Dunne J. 

 Charleton J. 

 Hogan J. 

 Murray J. 

 Collins J. 

   

 BETWEEN 

 G.M. 

 Applicant/Appellant 

 AND 

 I.M. 

 Respondent 

 AND 

 THE ATTORNEY GENERAL 

 Notice Party 

   

 JUDGMENT of Mr. Justice Maurice Collins delivered on 23 January 2026 

 

 1.                   I agree that this appeal should be dismissed and in large measure I agree with the detailed analysis and conclusions of Dunne J. On the central issue raised in this appeal - whether Isaac Wunder orders may be made in family law proceedings and, if so, in what circumstances and subject to what conditions - I agree completely with Dunne J's reasoning and conclusions. So far from excluding the exercise of the Isaac Wunder jurisdiction in family law litigation, consideration of the best interests of the child may well justify the making of such an order. More broadly, it is an unfortunate fact that family law proceedings can too often become a form of lawfare, in which the processes of the court are misused by one party to oppress, harass and destabilise the other. 

   

 2.                   The existence of such a jurisdiction, and its proper exercise in the area of family law, does not in my view, amount to any impermissible interference with, or limitation of, the right of access to the courts . Access to the courts is a fundamental constitutional right of every person within the jurisdiction, whether or not a citizen: Brandley v Deane [2017] IESC 83 , [2018] 2 IR 741, per McKechnie J at §48. However, there is no right to use the court's process to reopen litigation or to pursue litigation that is plainly groundless and vexatious: Riordan v Ireland (No 4) [2001] 3 IR 365 . Furthermore, the making of an Isaac Wunder order does not exclude access to court but rather makes recourse to the court subject to the court's prior permission. That has been characterised as " a proportionate filtering mechanism " intended " to protect the opposing party from the injustice of having to incur what are often very significant and unrecoverable costs, in meeting oppressive and abusive claims ": Fitzsimons v Bank of Scotland Plc [2019] IECA 336, per Noonan J at § 24. 

   

 3.                   Costs are not, of course, the only burden of litigation. It can also impose a heavy psychological toll on those involved and that is perhaps particularly true of family law litigation. In addition to the burden on litigants, witnesses and the other actors in the litigation process, vexatious and abusive claims impose a significant burden on the administration of justice. The protection of the public interest - in the finality of litigation and the proper use of limited court resources - is an important element of the Isaac Wunder jurisdiction and serves to explain why Issaac Wunder orders may be made by a court of its own motion: Houston v Doyle [2020] IECA 289 , §64 & §69. 

   

 4.                   I agree with Dunne J that the existence and/or exercise of the Isaac Wunder jurisdiction in family law litigation is not, in principle, contrary to Articles 6 and/or 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights (ECHR). 

   

 5.                   The power to make an Isaac Wunder order is one of the " inherent powers " that all courts enjoy as a necessary incident of their status and function as a court established by or under the Constitution: see the discussion of inherent powers in my judgment in Kirwan v Connors [2025] IESC 21 , at §34 and following. It is one of the powers that a court must have " in order to maintain its character as a court of justice ":  Bhamjee v Forsdick (Practice Note)   [2003] EWCA Civ 1113 , [2004] 1 WLR 88 , at 93. Bhamjee v Forsdick traces the recognition of such a power back to the judgment of Alderson B in Cocker v Tempest (1841) 7 M & W 502 ( §503-504) at 92. 

   

 6.                   The UK Parliament enacted the Vexatious Actions Act in 1896 (" the 1896 Act ") (now section 42 of the Senior Courts Act 1981) but the 1896 Act did not apply to Ireland. [1] This Court's decision in Wunder v Hospitals Trust (1940) Ltd (Unreported, 11 April 1967) appears to be the first time that an Irish court has made what has come to be labelled as an " Isaac Wunder order ". [2] But there is no single form of order and in practice such orders vary significantly in their terms. 

   

 7.                   Here, the order made by the Court of Appeal restrains GM from instituting any proceedings against IM, including any appeal, in any court (other than this Court), without the prior leave of the President of the court concerned (or his or her nominee), for an indefinite period. That is, on any view, a very broad form of order, corresponding to what in England and Wales is designated a General Civil Restraint Order . The need for such an order was first identified by the Court of Appeal of England and Wales in Bhamjee v Forsdick (Practice Note) : §§43-47. Notably, the Court of Appeal indicated that such an order should not be made for a period exceeding two years, unless subsequently extended: §46. Further provision for the making of such orders has been made by way of the Civil Procedure Rules (CPR) and Practice Direction ( Practice Direction 3C - Civil Restraint Orders ), which provides that such an order should not be made for a period in excess of three years but may be extended (again, for no more than three years). The CPR and the Practice Direction prescribe how applications for civil restraint orders are to be made, how applications for permission to bring proceedings are to be made and dealt with, the form of order to be made, and various related matters. Such orders are subject to different thresholds and differ significantly in their scope and effect. As well as General Civil Restraint Orders, these procedures allow for and regulate the making of other restraint orders of narrower scope, namely Limited Civil Restraint Orders (the effect of which is to prohibit a litigant from making any further applications in existing proceedings without prior permission) and Extended Civil Restraint Orders (the effect of which is to restrain the bringing of further proceedings relating to a specific issue or subject-matter). Extended Civil Restraint Orders are also subject to a three-year maximum limit, with the possibility of extension. 

   

 8.                   In this jurisdiction, there has not been any legislative intervention, nor has the Superior Courts Rules Committee made rules relating to the exercise of the Isaac Wunder jurisdiction. Whereas previously it may have been the case that Isaac Wunder orders were made only " in very rare circumstances " ( O' Malley v Irish Nationwide Building Society  (Unreported, High Court, Costello J, 21 January 1994), anyone involved in the administration of justice in Ireland - and the phenomenon is by no means unique to this jurisdiction - will be well aware that such orders are now sought, and made, with ever increasing frequency. [3] There appears to be no reason to believe that that trend will not continue. 

   

 9.                   In my view, it is high time that rules are made that regulate and structure this jurisdiction . Such rules could usefully set out the procedures for making an order (including the procedure applicable where a court considers it appropriate to make an order on its own initiative), the different kinds of order that may be made, the respective thresholds for making such orders, their duration, the name of such orders - the name " Isaac Wunder order " may have historical resonance but gives no clue as to the nature of such an order and in fact covers a multitude of different orders, with significantly different impacts on litigants - the manner in which the making of such orders should be recorded (and the circumstances in which that record should be made accessible to the public, which may require consideration of data protection law) and how applications for permission to litigate should be dealt with. Such rules could also address appeal rights. 

   

 10.               Given that the power to make such orders is an inherent or implied power, there would appear to be no reason why that power cannot be regulated by rules adopted by the Superior Courts Rules Committee: see my judgment in Kirwan v Connors , §44. That is not to say that there might not be value in legislative intervention, such as by the enactment of a provision similar to section 41 of the (UK) Senior Courts Act 1981 and/or more generally to address disruptive behaviour in or in the vicinity of courts. But primary legislation does not appear to be necessary to address many of the issues that arise in relation to so-called Isaac Wunder orders. 

   

 11.               There are two particular aspects of Dunne J's judgment that I wish to briefly address. The first concerns the question whether - and if so on what basis - the High Court may make litigation restraint orders - Isaac Wunder orders - in respect of proceedings before the Circuit Court or District Court. The second relates to the power of those courts to make such orders in respect of proceedings before them. 

   

 12.               As regards the first of these issues, I agree with Dunne J that the High Court (and, on appeal, the Court of Appeal and this Court) may make orders regulating the commencement and/or maintenance of proceedings in the Circuit and District Courts. The rationale for such a jurisdiction was articulated by the Court of Appeal of England and Wales in Ebert v Venvil [2000] Ch 484 , at 498, as follows: 

   

 "The High Court has traditionally exercised a supervisory jurisdiction in relation to the county court and although that jurisdiction is normally exercised over the county court by means of judicial review this does not mean that it is the only way the jurisdiction can be exercised. It could for example properly be exercised by the granting of an injunction or by the sort of orders made by Neuberger J. If authority was needed for this it is provided by In re Connolly Brothers Ltd. [1911] 1 Ch 731 . In that case the proceedings which were restrained were in the Lancaster Palatine Court and not a county court. In addition the proceedings had already been commenced when they were restrained. Furthermore the injunction would be enforceable against the individual and not the court. None the less these distinctions do not alter the principle involved. The county court will give effect to the High Court order in the same way as it would give effect to an order made by a county court judge. We still have a High Court and county courts with separate but overlapping jurisdictions. However both courts are part of the same civil justice system." 

   

 13.               Here, as in England and Wales, the supervisory jurisdiction of the High Court in respect of the Circuit and District Courts is normally exercised by means of judicial review. But the jurisdiction is a broader one, as is illustrated by the undoubted power of the High Court to punish contempt before, and of, the Circuit or District Court (as to which see R v Davies [1906] 1 KB 32 , AG v O' Ryan and Boyd [1946] IR 70, AG v Connolly [1947] IR 213 and State (DPP) v Walsh & Conneely [1981] IR 412), as well as its long-established power to grant injunctive relief restraining the commencement or maintenance of proceedings in the Circuit or District Court, or staying such proceedings (as to which see the discussion at §§12-15 of the judgment of Murray J). 

   

 14.               As regards Clune v Director of Public Prosecutions [1981] ILRM 17, I do not find it easy to understand the point being made by Gannon J in the passage set out by Murray J in his judgment (§§20-21). The Circuit and District Courts are indeed subject to direction, control and supervision by the High Court. Indeed, in Clune there appears to have been no dispute but that the High Court had the power to grant the relief sought by the prosecutor (injunction/prohibition directed to the District Court) - the issue was that the evidence was insufficient to support the making of such orders on a quia timet basis. Read literally, the statement that District Judges are free " from purported intervention, direction or control by any superior court " is not just inconsistent with the fact that such Judges are subject to judicial review, but is also inconsistent with the exercise by the High Court of any Isaac Wunder type jurisdiction in respect of proceedings before the Circuit Court or the District Court  a jurisdiction that all members of the Court agree exist, even if there is some disagreement as to its basis. 

   

 15.               Accordingly, in my view, the jurisdiction of the High Court - a jurisdiction rooted in the first instance in Article 34.3.1° of the Constitution but also encompassing the jurisdiction transferred to the High Court by section 8(2) of the Courts (Supplemental Provisions) Act 1961 - extends to making orders of the kind made here (albeit that the  order at issue here was in fact made on appeal by the Court of Appeal). That jurisdiction does not constitute the High Court as " custos mores " nor is its existence contingent on the High Court having any such function. Furthermore, on my analysis, that jurisdiction does not duplicate the jurisdiction enjoyed by the Circuit and District Courts because it is materially more extensive than such jurisdiction. 

   

 16.               The exercise of that jurisdiction would also be assisted by the making of appropriate rules by the Superior Courts Rules Committee. 

   

 17.               I turn now to the second issue, in respect of which I differ from my colleagues. In the first place, I would locate the power of the Circuit and District Court to make Isaac Wunder type orders exclusively in the implied power of those courts - courts of record established under the Constitution and charged with the administration of justice - to supervise and control their own processes. I agree with Murray J that the rationale for such a power is well-captured in the passage from Abbott J's judgment in SP v UG [2016] IEHC 693 to which he refers (§3). I do not consider that such a power arises from either section 22(1)(a) or section 22(6) of the Courts (Supplemental Provisions) Act 1961 (which are in my view concerned with the substantive jurisdiction of the Circuit Court) or section 22(7) of that Act (the language of which is not, in my view, apt to encompass the making of an Isaac Wunder order, as such an order is not ancillary to any jurisdiction exercisable by the Circuit Court in the sense contemplated in section 22(7)). As Murray J observes in his judgment (§12), section 22 effectively re-enacts provisions first contained in the Courts of Justice Act 1924 and it appears distinctly implausible that the Oireachtas intended to confer such a power on the Circuit Court in 1924 (or, for that matter, in 1961) before  it was ever established that the Superior Courts had such a power. That is particularly so if, as my colleagues appear to consider, the power so conferred extends to the making of an order restraining the commencement of any proceedings potentially against any party in any Circuit in the State. I would also observe that, if the power to make such an order derives from section 22 of the 1961 Act, as opposed to being an inherent/implied power, it would seem necessarily to follow that the District Court does not have any such power, in the absence of any statutory equivalent to section 22(1)(a), (6) and/or (7). 

   

 18.               There may be " only one Circuit Court in the State and only one District Court " (per Walsh J in State (Boyle) v Neylon [1986] IR 551, at 555-556) but the structure and organisation of those courts differs significantly from the High Court. Indeed, the State (Boyle) v Neylon illustrates that fact. Notwithstanding that the Circuit Court was " a single court for the whole State " (per Walsh J at 556) the transfer of a criminal trial to the Dublin Circuit was possible only because the Oireachtas had expressly provided for it. 

   

 19.               The exercise of the jurisdiction of the Circuit and District Courts on a local basis is a key aspect of their statutory architecture, underpinned by the provisions of Article 34.3.4° of the Constitution. The legal relationship between judges of the Circuit Court inter se , and between such judges and the President of the Circuit Court differs significantly from the position in the High Court. That is also true of the District Court. 

   

 20.               Having regard to these legal and constitutional realities, it seems to me that the requirements of justice are adequately met by recognising the power of Judges of the Circuit and District Courts to make litigation restraint orders - Isaac Wunder orders - in relation to their respective Circuits and Districts only. It may be permissible for a broader power to be conferred on the Circuit and District Courts by primary legislation or by rules made by their respective rules committees (though that would require careful consideration of the restrictions flowing from Article 34.3.4°) but in my view any inherent or implied power should reflect and respect the basic structure of these courts. In arriving at that conclusion I am not, I hope, guilty of confusing or conflating the (local and limited) jurisdiction of the Circuit and District Courts with the breadth of orders that may be made by judges of those Courts when seized with jurisdiction. In my view, the jurisdiction at issue here is materially different: in the first place, it is an implied or inherent jurisdiction, rather than one conferred by statute; secondly, the jurisdiction is not concerned - or at least primarily concerned - with the adjudication of inter partes disputes nor is its exercise contingent on the posture of the parties; thirdly   and importantly - it is a constitutionally sensitive jurisdiction, given its impact on the fundamental right of access to the courts. 

   

 21.               I am not persuaded that it is a necessary incident of the respective status and functions of the Circuit and District Courts that they should have a power to make " nationwide " Issac Wunder orders (even limited to their respective courts), such that such a power is to be recognised as an implied or inherent power. Of course, limiting the power to make Isaac Wunder orders to proceedings within a particular District or Circuit will leave open the possibility of a litigant seeking to circumvent the order by bringing proceedings in some other District or Circuit. But jurisdictional rules limit that possibility and any abuse can be dealt with readily by the court whose jurisdiction has been invoked. 

   

 22.               In any event, as I have said, if it is considered necessary or desirable that the Circuit Court and the District Court should have power to make " nationwide " orders, it seems to me that such a power would have to be conferred by law, subject of course to Article 34.3.4° (such a law would also have to deal with the practical incidents and consequences of such a jurisdiction, in terms of maintaining a record of orders made and providing for the procedures of seeking consent to commence proceedings and by whom such consent may be given). The precise effect of that constitutional limitation is a matter for another day's debate. Any such debate will be informed by this Court's decision in Permanent TSB v Langan [2017] IESC 71 , [2018] 1 IR 375 but that decision is not, and does not purport to be, the last word on that subject (§77). It is clear from Permanent TSB v Langan that a " real meaning must be given to the requirement that the jurisdiction of a court such as the Circuit Court is limited " (§74) and that the Circuit Court (and a fortiori the District Court) " cannot become a surrogate court of full original jurisdiction " (§77). Clarke CJ was careful to stress that the category of case at issue in Permanent TSB v Langan was " relatively narrow ", relating to a " limited class of property " (§75). While it was not necessary for the Court to identify the threshold for determining whether any particular category of case was so broad that jurisdiction to deal with it might not permissibly be conferred on the Circuit Court, it is clear that, as a matter of principle, such a limit follows from Article 34.3.4° (§77). Were it necessary to identify that threshold or limit, in addition to considering the breadth of the jurisdiction concerned, its nature and constitutional significance would also appear to be essential considerations. 

   

 23.               Subject to the foregoing, I agree with the judgment of Dunne J and agree that this appeal should be dismissed, and the Order of the Court of Appeal affirmed.     [1] m Taggart, " Alexander Chaffers and the Genesis of the Vexatious Actions Act 1896" (2004) 63 The Cambridge Law Journal 656-684 provides an entertaining account of the background to the enactment of the 1896 Act. 

 [2] Notably, no authority was cited in Wunder . While Grepe v Loam (1887) 37 Ch D 168 has been cited by Irish courts on a number of occasions, all such references are recent and long post-date the decision in Wunder . 

 [3] See generally McCarthy, "Frivolous and Vexatious Litigation in the Irish Courts: Challenges, Remedies, and Reform" (2025) Irish Judicial Studies Journal Vol 9(1) 173-198.
